title: Eating Light
principle: Making food out of air and light is called photosynthesis.

t: A tree weighs tonnes. Almost none of that came out of the ground.
An oak weighs several tonnes, and the soil around it is not several tonnes lighter. Nearly all of that mass arrived from somewhere else.
sub: So where did a tree come from?
The answer was got wrong for two thousand years, and settling it took one careful experiment.

question: Where does most of a tree's weight come from?
What is the principal source of a tree's dry mass?
note: Guess before you look. Almost everybody gets this wrong.
Commit. Van Helmont weighed a willow and its pot for five years in the 1640s and concluded it was the water — which was closer than the received view and still wrong.

stages.label: Where the wood came from

Van Helmont's willow, and what it did and did not establish.
after: A tree is mostly air. That is a very strange sentence and it is true.
Dry mass is roughly half carbon, and every carbon atom arrived as atmospheric CO₂. The soil supplies minerals in small quantities and almost none of the bulk.

t: Making food out of air and light is called photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide and water, plus light energy, assembled into sugar. Oxygen is the leftover.
6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Light energy is captured and stored in chemical bonds; the oxygen is a by-product of splitting water, not of the carbon dioxide.

The oxygen comes from the water rather than the CO₂, which was settled by isotope labelling in 1941 and is not obvious from the equation. Every oxygen molecule you have ever breathed was pulled off a water molecule by a plant, an alga or a cyanobacterium.
sub: The oxygen you breathe is what plants throw away.
Oxygen is waste. The atmosphere you depend on is the discarded by-product of somebody else's chemistry.
It accumulated over hundreds of millions of years and was, for the organisms already here, a catastrophe.

The Great Oxidation Event was a mass extinction caused by pollution — oxygen is corrosive, and the anaerobic life it poisoned had no defence. Everything that breathes it now descends from whatever survived.

q: What is a tree mostly made of?
What is the source of the carbon in wood?
Where does the carbon in a tree's dry mass originate?
options: Carbon that used to be in the air
Minerals it pulled up from the soil
Water it soaked up through its roots
why: Every bit of wood is built from carbon dioxide the tree took out of the air. The soil gives it a few minerals and holds it upright, and that is nearly all.

Wood is roughly half carbon by dry mass, and all of that carbon entered as atmospheric CO₂. Soil contributes minerals in trace quantities — which is why a hydroponically grown plant does perfectly well with no soil at all.

The soil supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and trace elements in small amounts; the bulk is atmospheric carbon fixed by the Calvin cycle. This is also why afforestation is a carbon sink in a literal rather than metaphorical sense — the carbon is structurally in the tree.

t: Almost every scrap of energy in every living thing started as sunlight caught by a plant.

Photosynthesis is the entry point for essentially all energy in the biosphere. Your lunch, the animal that ate the plant, the coal in a power station and the oil in a tanker are all the same store — sunlight banked in chemical bonds, some of it this year and some of it three hundred million years ago.
